Main.unitMcgDesc: One millionth of a gram (1/1000 mg). Used for microelements that the body requires in microscopic doses but possess colossal biological activity. For instance, the daily value of vital Vitamin D3 (20 mcg) is visually smaller than a single grain of sand, and Vitamin B12 status is measured precisely in mcg.
Main.unitMgDesc: One thousandth of a gram. This is the baseline measure for most vitamins and minerals. To help you visualize: a standard vitamin C tablet is typically 50-100 mg. Milligrams measure your daily requirements for Iron, Zinc, as well as macrominerals like Calcium and Magnesium (which are needed in larger amounts — around 400-1000 mg).
Main.unitGDesc: The primary unit of weight. Grams are used exclusively for macronutrients (Proteins, Fats, Carbohydrates) and dietary fiber. The total weight of food items in the app is also displayed in grams. Remember that 1 gram of fat provides 9 kcal, while 1 gram of protein or carbs provides 4 kcal.
Main.unitDvDesc: The ultimate guide for reading nutritional data. It shows what percentage of the average adult's daily requirement is supplied by one serving. Apply the golden rule: if a nutrient is ≤ 5% DV, the food is low in it; if it is ≥ 20% DV (like the 22% in the example above), it is considered an excellent, high-potency source.
Main.unitMeDesc: Measures biological activity rather than physical weight. Different forms of a vitamin have different weights, but IU standardizes their potency. Most commonly used for Vitamins D, A, and E. For example, 400 IU of Vitamin D3 is exactly equal to 10 mcg.

Article.title: The pros and cons of fast food
Article.intro: Fast food is convenient and affordable, but regular consumption affects energy, weight, and long-term health. Here is a balanced look at what it offers and what to watch for.
Article.pros1: Quick and convenient when you are short on time.
Article.pros2: Predictable portions and calories on many menus.
Article.pros3: Affordable option compared with many sit-down restaurants.
Article.cons1: Often high in salt, sugar, and unhealthy fats.
Article.cons2: Low in fiber and micronutrients compared with whole foods.
Article.cons3: Frequent intake is linked to weight gain and higher cardiovascular risk.
Article.outro: Occasional fast food is fine for most people. For everyday nutrition, prioritize vegetables, fruits, lean proteins, and home-cooked meals from the product catalog.
